messages:
alex-cust: Hey team — since yesterday our Redwood Private control plane connections started failing during TLS handshake after we applied a proxy firmware update. API calls from our VPC to controlplane.redwood.internal are getting TLS alerts and the control plane rejects the ClientHello. Here's the short client log: 
```
Status: TLS handshake failed: alert handshake_failure
err=1408A10B:SSL routines:ssl3_get_client_hello:no shared cipher
```
We didn't change certs on our side. Any hints?

lina-support: Thanks Alex — can you confirm the exact control plane hostname/IP you're hitting and whether you have SSL inspection (TLS MITM) on the egress proxy/firewall? Also any recent NAT/load-balancer changes? :eyes:

alex-cust: Hostname is controlplane.redwood.internal -> 10.12.45.22 (private peering). We do have a corporate SSL-inspecting proxy (Palo Alto NGFW) that was upgraded at 02:00 UTC yesterday. Network team says it's doing TLS interception, re-signing with their CA. No LB changes.

raj-infra: Can you paste a minimal tcpdump of the first few packets (SYN, SYN-ACK, and first TLS ClientHello bytes)? Looking for fragmentation/truncation. A sample command: `sudo tcpdump -s 0 -w - host 10.12.45.22 and port 443` or a hexdump of the ClientHello. MTU fragmentation between client and proxy sometimes causes ClientHello truncation that breaks mTLS.

alex-cust: Pasting sanitized tcpdump/openssl output — we can't share full pcap here but here's the ClientHello visible from our side (via `openssl s_client -connect 10.12.45.22:443 -servername controlplane.redwood.internal -msg`):
```
>>> TLS 1.3 Handshake, ClientHello
Version: 0x0303
Random: <snip>
Session ID: <empty>
Cipher Suites: TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, ...
Extensions:
  server_name: controlplane.redwood.internal
  signature_algorithms
  key_share
  supported_versions
  supported_groups
  application_layer_protocol_negotiation: http/1.1, h2
>>> send raw, 512 bytes
<<< TLS 1.3 Alert, fatal, handshake_failure
```
We also captured from the proxy side and see the proxy rewrites server_name to shorter hostname (they claim) and truncates SNI in some cases.

sam-sre: That SNI truncation + SSL-inspection combo would definitely break mTLS if the control plane expects a full SNI and client cert context. Two quick repros: (1) try `openssl s_client -connect 10.12.45.22:443 -servername controlplane.redwood.internal -cert client.pem -key client.key -state -msg` from a host that bypasses the proxy (if available) and see if handshake completes; (2) curl with `--http2 -v --resolve 'controlplane.redwood.internal:443:10.12.45.22' --cert client.pem --key client.key https://controlplane.redwood.internal/health` and compare. If bypass works, it's egress inspection.

maya-eng: Also check whether the proxy is munging ALPN or client certificate chains. Our Private control plane requires SNI intact + ALPN (http/1.1 or h2) and full client cert chain for mutual TLS. If any of those are rewritten, the server will send handshake_failure. Requesting these items from your network team:
- tcpdump showing ClientHello bytes leaving your app host (first 1KB)
- tcpdump on the egress device showing the ClientHello it forwards toward 10.12.45.22
- `openssl s_client -showcerts` output for the failed attempt

alex-cust: Got an extra trace from the NGFW team — they captured the forwarded packet and it shows ClientHello length 256 and SNI truncated to "controlplane.red" (they have a rule that truncates SNI > 32 bytes during intercept). Attaching snippet: 
```
Forwarded ClientHello: server_name: controlplane.red
ALPN: http/1.1
ClientCert: present (re-signed by corp-CA)
```
We suspect the NGFW re-signing + SNI truncation is the culprit.

lina-support: That matches our expectation. The control plane validates SNI to map incoming connection to the proper tenant cert and routing. If SNI is truncated, routing fails and we drop the handshake. Two remediation paths: (A) allow passthrough (disable SSL intercept) for that destination IP or domain, or (B) have the NGFW preserve full SNI and ALPN and not re-write the client cert when connecting to Redwood Private control plane.

raj-infra: Quick checklist for support ticket:
- Capture from host: `sudo tcpdump -s 200 -nn -A host 10.12.45.22 and port 443` (first KB)
- Capture from NGFW egress interface showing altered ClientHello
- `openssl s_client -connect 10.12.45.22:443 -servername controlplane.redwood.internal -cert client.pem -key client.key -showcerts` (both from bypass and behind proxy)
- Confirm NGFW rule name that does SNI rewrite + its configured max SNI length

alex-cust: I'll collect those and escalate to our network team. One more question — any temporary workaround on Redwood side? Can you accept truncated SNI or fallback?

maya-eng: We can't accept truncated SNI for tenant routing because it's how we mux TLS connections. We can add a policy to accept an alternate CN if you want, but that requires an auth change and rollout on our side (not ideal for immediate). Fastest path is to whitelist controlplane.redwood.internal in your egress policy so the NGFW does not intercept.

infra-bot: Ticket created: RED-INC-8721 — Escalation: mTLS handshake failures caused by egress SSL-inspection SNI truncation. Assigned: raj-infra, maya-eng.

alex-cust: Network team disabled SSL inspection for the IP and I can confirm the handshake succeeds now from our hosts. `curl --cert client.pem --key client.key https://controlplane.redwood.internal/health` returns 200. Will follow up with them to make the allowlist permanent. :white_check_mark:

lina-support: Great — marking this thread as resolved for now. Please ping if anything reappears or if you want us to implement an alternate tenant CN mapping.

alex-cust: Thanks everyone, really appreciate the quick help.
